item.title: Terminal-state theorems for a two-stage Maki--Thompson rumor model: final size, stifler composition, and non-identifiability from pooled statistics
item.description: arXiv:2610.41206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rumor models of the Daley--Kendall and Maki--Thompson family anchor the statistical mechanics of social contagion, yet the stifler composition a rumor leaves behind has resisted closed-form analysis. Inspired by the asymmetric two-step pairing (A2SP) process of step-growth polymerization, we import its common-factor cancellation into a minimal two-stage MT variant in which re-contacted spreaders are re-activated into a senior class at rate $\alpha k_1$ rather than stifled, and obtain exact terminal-state theorems. (i) Saturation: the rumor exhausts the ignorant pool for every stifling-to-recruitment ratio $\mu>0$, with a three-way tail classification and a logarithmically critical line at $\mu=1$. (ii) Final size: the terminal stifler pool splits as $(x_1,x_2)=(\mu/(\alpha+\mu),\alpha/(\alpha+\mu))$, independent of seed size; the fingerprint inverts linearly ($\alpha=\mu x_2/x_1$) and matches Gillespie simulations within $0.95\%$. (iii) Pooled versus history-resolved: pooled statistics are exactly $\alpha$-free on any static graph; only the history-resolved composition carries $\alpha$. Restoring the classic teller-retires channel breaks the exact closure beyond quantified gates (contact rates of $1$--$3\%$ of $k_1$ for spreader channels at $\mu\leq1.5$, up to $32\%$ at $\mu=2$), and on configuration-model networks the composition bias decays as $\langle k\rangle^{-0.71}$. An exploratory inversion of 354,930 Higgs--Twitter retweet episodes, screened by an identity check and four negative controls, yields $\hat{\alpha}=2.21\%$ (joint cluster-bootstrap CI $[1.6\%,3.0\%]$; $\approx3.7\%$ after calibration at the matched threshold). Terminal compositions identify this effective re-activation rate, an upper bound on contact-coupled re-activation; the mechanism itself requires timing information beyond the terminal state.
item.dc:creator: Qingquan Tang

item.title: Understanding LLM-Based Bargaining of Driving Agents in Mixed-Autonomy Traffic
item.description: arXiv:2610.41239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a flexible computational approach for modeling social interactions among heterogeneous agents. This paper develops a novel framework towards characterizing and understanding LLM-based population-level bargaining of shared road space between autonomous vehicle (AV) and human-driven vehicle (HV) agents in mixed-autonomy traffic. Through controlled experiments varying traffic density, agent objectives, and traffic-domain knowledge, we first characterize bargaining outcomes and observe heterogeneous agreement rates across different experimental conditions. To understand how the bargaining process shapes the outcomes, we introduce a behavioral taxonomy that jointly characterizes numerical bidding actions and communicative attitudes. We examine two complementary aspects of social interaction: inter-agent bargaining dynamics and private-to-public behavioral transformation. Results reveal distinct interaction patterns associated with agreement and breakdown, including greater constructive reciprocity in agreement trials and more frequent conflict escalation in breakdown trials. Furthermore, private and public communicative attitudes often differ even when numerical bids remain unchanged. These findings illustrate how LLM-based bargaining simulations can support a structured analysis of social interaction behaviors in mixed-autonomy traffic.
item.dc:creator: Lingxiao Zhou, Di Chen, Jia Li

item.title: Why delivered costs understate prices in an integrated global hydrogen market
item.description: arXiv:2610.41447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delivered-cost estimates are often used as proxies for hydrogen import prices. Yet they measure average supply-chain costs, whereas marginal prices measure the system value of an additional unit. Market interactions can make the two diverge, potentially biasing long-term price assumptions. We quantify this gap using an 81-region global hydrogen-market model, comparing each region's costs and prices when only its demand is active and when all regions' demands are active. The 2045 price-cost gap is positive in 78 regions and averages 63 EUR/MWh (52% of the single-buyer cost) on a demand-weighted basis. Only 12 EUR/MWh reflects higher average sourcing costs due to competing demand. The remaining 51 EUR/MWh is the difference between the global-market price and the delivered portfolio's average cost. In several regions, wholesale prices rise while average delivered costs fall. Hydrogen strategies should distinguish delivered-cost benchmarks from market-price expectations, as low-cost supply does not guarantee low regional market prices.
item.dc:creator: Bastian Wei{\ss}enburger, Martin Wietschel, Patrick Pl\"otz, Russell McKenna

item.title: Resonant Amplification of Demographic Noise in Stochastic Common-Pool Resource Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.41830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Common-pool resources are vulnerable to overexploitation, yet many social-ecological systems exhibit persistent oscillations. We introduce a stochastic eco-evolutionary model in which harvesting strategies and resource availability shape one another. In the infinite population limit the system approaches a stable state through damped oscillations. Demographic noise continually excites these modes, generating instead robust macroscopic quasi-cycles, whose frequencies depend on the noise ratio, the relative timescale between strategy and resource, and the harvesting pressure. The model reproduces the distinct frequency peaks, observed in empirical global fish-landings data for high- and low-income countries, showing that persistent environmental fluctuations can emerge naturally from demographic noise.
item.dc:creator: Susanna C. Caruso, Fabio Menegazzo, Vito Latora, Samir Suweis

item.title: Combinatorial Calculations of the Most Probable Short-term Return of Single Company Stocks on the Stock Market
item.description: arXiv:2610.41979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The combinatorial method is used to calculate the quantity of distribution variants for the number of stockholders of one individual company as well as the quantity of stocks in the stockholder portfolio. These quantities may change as a result of the stocks buy and sale that is taken into account also. The total number of stocks the units at the lower level of the problem is obviously preserved, while the number of portfolios - the structural units at the upper level may change. The most probable distributions of the number of portfolios and stocks in each of them are determined depending on the expense to add a stock to the portfolio (the purchase price). The application of the developed method to determine the most probable short term return on stocks in a combinatorial sense is demonstrated.
item.dc:creator: Michael Romanovsky

item.title: Recommendation Feedback Loops Shape Urban Income Segregation and Venue Visitation
item.description: arXiv:2610.41911v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Location-based recommender systems shape where people go in cities and learn from the visits they steer, forming a human-AI feedback loop. This feedback loop shapes whom people share places with across income groups and which venues keep attracting customers. Yet platforms judge these systems by their offline accuracy on past visits, a test in which the suggestions never change where people go and which therefore cannot capture long-term effects. Studying these effects in cities is challenging because, unlike online resources, travel constraints and limited venue capacity shape where people can go, while each recommended visit also changes whom other visitors encounter. To capture such features, we build a long-term simulation framework based on fine-grained human mobility data from four U.S. metropolitan areas, with distance and capacity constraints. Focusing on food venues, we study two urban consequences: how unevenly people's exposure is distributed across income groups (experienced income segregation) and the share of venues receiving no visits from simulated residents (venue disappearance). We find that, under every algorithm and in every metropolitan area, at least a fifth of venues stop receiving visits, and that more than half of this loss arises from retraining. More importantly, more accurate algorithms leave people more segregated, and the most accurate algorithm leaves people 15-21% more segregated than they actually are. We then test a re-ranking intervention that favours less popular venues and runs on top of a platform's existing algorithm. It lowers both venue disappearance and segregation across algorithms, largely without directing people to venues where they may feel less comfortable. Our results suggest that impact assessments of recommender systems should account for the feedback loop and report segregation and venue disappearance beyond accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Guangyuan Weng, Lin Chen, Ciro Beneduce, Giovanni Mauro, Massimiliano Luca, Takahiro Yabe, Bruno Lepri, Luca Pappalardo, Esteban Moro

item.title: The joint dynamics of Personal, Expressed and Social beliefs
item.description: arXiv:2502.14362v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding belief dynamics is essential for dealing with societal phenomena from misperceptions and conflicts to polarization and stalemates in collective action. However, it is impeded by two main challenges. First, rich and largely qualitative knowledge about socio-cognitive processes involved in belief change and spread is insufficiently integrated into computational models of belief dynamics. Second, while numerous models of belief dynamics exist, they are rarely compared because of the differences in underlying theoretical frameworks and modeling choices. Here we address these two problems by developing a Personal, Expressed, and Social Beliefs (PES) meta-model in which personal beliefs co-evolve with one's expressed beliefs and perceived beliefs of others. It formalizes many critical socio-cognitive processes including authenticity, self-reinforcement, ego projection, social influence, conformity, validity, context effects, inertia, and potential and felt dissonance. It also enables principled comparison of a wide range of existing belief-dynamics models as its nested versions, from Voter, Ising, and DeGroot models, to bounded confidence and belief network models. We show how PES can be used to compare possible mechanisms underlying pluralistic ignorance, and find that it can occur when people conform their expressed beliefs to perceived beliefs of others, in particular when they have limited expressive repertoire (e.g., like, dislike, or stay silent). Counterintuitively, pluralistic ignorance can be dissolved when everyone ego-projects their own personal beliefs onto others to the same extent. Ego-projection generates misperception only when it is heterogeneous and covaries with personal beliefs. These results yield testable hypotheses and help predict when interventions will change personal, expressed, or social beliefs.
item.dc:creator: Filippo Zimmaro, Mirta Galesic, Henrik Olsson

item.title: Green building blocks reveal the complex anatomy of climate change mitigation technologies
item.description: arXiv:2504.06834v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Achieving net-zero emissions requires rapid innovation, yet the necessary technological knowhow is scattered across industries and countries. Comparing functionally similar green and nongreen patents, we identify "Green Building Blocks" (GBBs): modular components that can be added to reduce existing technologies' carbon footprints. These GBBs depict the anatomy of the green transition as a network that connects problems --- nongreen technologies --- to GBBs that mitigate their climate-change impact. Node degrees in this network are highly unequal, showing that the scope for climate-change mitigating innovation varies substantially across domains. The network helps predict which green technologies firms develop and maps which organizations hold complementary capabilities. The most complementary potential partners reside abroad for 84% of US firms, 87% of German firms, and 92% of Chinese firms, highlighting the importance of being able to collaborate across national borders.
item.dc:creator: Yang Li, Frank Neffke

item.title: FLAT: Smoothing the Rugged Landscape for Learnable, Sample-Efficient Traffic Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2610.04337v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Calibrating microscopic traffic models for digital twins is an expensive black-box optimization problem: tuning car-following and lane-changing parameters requires a full simulation run, affording only a tight budget per recalibration window. Matching raw trajectories yields a rugged objective that sparse surrogates cannot learn, reducing sequential acquisition to near-random probing. We present FLAT, which couples what to optimize with where to sample next. An eight-dimensional behavioral fingerprint smooths the parameter-error landscape, making the objective learnable from a few dozen samples; annealed lower-confidence-bound (LCB) acquisition then spends each remaining run where it most reduces error. The surrogate, interchangeable among a Gaussian process (GP), random forest (RF), or multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) ensemble, plugs into the same LCB loop. Across six heterogeneous real-world scenes, FLAT-GP achieves the lowest scene-averaged behavioral error, winning 6/6 scenes against SPSA, GA, and CMA-ES and 5/6 against TPE under the matched budget. Some baselines need up to 4.4 times more simulations to match. Ablations show objective choice shifts final behavioral error by 81% on average, removing sequential LCB raises the six-scene mean by 20%, and surrogate choice shifts it by at most 4.2%, confirming gains trace to objective geometry and sequential allocation rather than surrogate capacity.
item.dc:creator: Haopeng Deng, Thomas He, Dayuan Wang

item.title: Emergence and coexistence of periodic and unstructured motion in future-avoiding random walks
item.description: arXiv:2602.03308v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Self-avoiding random walks on graphs can be seen as walkers interacting with their own past history. Here, we consider a complementary class of dynamics, mutual future-avoiding random walks (MFARWs), where stochastically driven walkers are avoiding each other's planned future trajectories. Such systems arise naturally in conceptual models of shared mobility. We show that periodic behavior emerges spontaneously in two different MFARWs, and that periodic and unstructured behavior coexist, providing an example of chimera like behavior of nonoscillatory paths on networks. Further, we analytically describe and predict the onset of structure. We find that the transition from unstructured to periodic behavior is driven by a mechanism of self-amplifying coupling to the periodic components of the stochastic drivers of the system. In the context of shared mobility applications, these states imply a regime of naturally stable coexistence between flexible and line-based public transport.
item.dc:creator: A. Schmaus, K. Stiller, N. Molkenthin
